t: Introduction: topic, aim and plan
n: In this lecture we will consider the forensic medical examination of cases of death arising from the effect of high temperature on the human body. The topic consists of two parts: the general effect of high temperature, that is heat stroke and sunstroke, and the local effect, that is thermal burn. According to the plan, heat exchange, degrees of burn, burn disease and the vitality of the action of flame are studied. The aim is that you master the basis for determining whether flame acted during life or after death on a corpse found after a fire. Remember: heat stroke is not sunstroke, but the morphological changes on the corpse are similar and non-specific, so there is a risk of error.

t: Body temperature and routes of heat loss
n: Normal body temperature is 36–37 °C. In metabolism heat is formed, and the body gives it off in a regulated way. The diagram shows the routes of heat loss: radiation 55 %, sweat 27 %, conduction 15 %, various secretions 3 %. If the temperature is below 22–25 °C or above 43–44 °C, changes incompatible with life occur in the tissues. That is, the body lives within a very narrow temperature range. The general effect of high temperature leads to heat stroke, and the local effect leads to a burn.

t: Damaging factors of high temperature and their types
n: The damaging factors of high temperature include a hot external environment, flame, combustible gases, liquids and solids. The types of action are shown in the diagram. The general action relates to the whole body, one form of which is heat stroke and another sunstroke, that is insolation. Sunstroke arises from prolonged action of the sun's rays on the head without headgear in an open place. In heat stroke, however, much heat is produced and little is given off. The local action causes a thermal burn.

t: Heat stroke: predisposing factors
n: Heat stroke develops when much heat is produced in the body and little is given off. The risk rises at high air temperature and humidity and with no wind. This is seen in hot workshops, in heavy physical work, and in training of athletes and soldiers. Clothing that does not pass air and moisture also predisposes. In cardiovascular disease, hyperfunction of the thyroid gland, obesity and old age, heat stroke is commoner. In children under one year the mechanisms of thermoregulation are not fully formed, so they are very sensitive to high temperature.

t: Mechanism of development of heat stroke
n: In the mechanism of heat stroke the main place is held by disturbance of haemodynamics: the blood thickens and circulation slows. This intensifies tissue hyperthermia still more and leads to tissue hypoxia. The chain continues as follows: haemodynamics is disturbed, the blood thickens, hyperthermia intensifies, hypoxia arises in the tissues and metabolism is disturbed. In the stress reaction catecholamines and glucocorticoids are released, and stasis occurs in the microcirculation.

t: Acute and protracted forms of heat stroke
n: Heat stroke occurs in two forms. In an unaccustomed, that is unacclimatised, body very high temperature causes the acute form. In this, consciousness is suddenly lost, coma develops, the cardiovascular and respiratory systems are sharply disturbed, and death occurs in a short time. In the protracted form the exposure is relatively longer, and the clinical signs and degree of severity increase gradually. The periods: depression, excitation and prostration. Prostration is regarded as the preagonal period.

t: The three periods of the protracted form
n: The protracted form consists of three periods. In the first period the activity of the central nervous system, that is the CNS, is depressed; this is a short latent period. The second is the period of excitation: restlessness, headache, tachycardia, raised blood pressure and dyspnoea are seen. The third is the period of prostration: temperature may exceed 41–42 °C, coma and convulsions occur, and this is the preagonal period. As a result, if body temperature exceeds 42–43 °C, breathing stops primarily.

t: Quick question: heat stroke
n: Let us test our knowledge. First question: how many periods are distinguished in protracted heat stroke? Answer: three, that is the periods of CNS depression, excitation and prostration. Second question: which period is regarded as preagonal? Answer: the period of prostration; in it coma, convulsions, slowing of breathing and fall of pressure are seen. Third question: above what temperature does death occur from primary cessation of breathing? Answer: when body temperature exceeds 42–43 °C. Fourth question: how does death proceed in the acute form? Answer: consciousness is suddenly lost, coma develops, and the cardiovascular and respiratory systems are sharply disturbed.

t: Sunstroke (insolation)
n: Sunstroke, that is insolation, develops in an open place, without headgear, when sunlight acts on the head for a long time. The head heats up and the central nervous system is seriously disturbed: headache, clouding of consciousness, visual disturbance, hallucinations and convulsions are seen. Pulse and breathing first quicken, then the pulse slows. Pathological breathing and paralysis of the respiratory centre are possible. Attention: in sunstroke body temperature does not rise significantly. On the skin there may be signs of a first-degree burn, that is erythema.

t: Comparing heat stroke and sunstroke
n: Now we compare the two conditions. Heat stroke develops when much heat is produced and little given off, especially in humid and windless air; the blood thickens, hypoxia arises, temperature may exceed 41–42 °C, and above 42–43 °C breathing stops. Sunstroke, however, arises from prolonged action of the sun's rays on the head without headgear in an open place; the head heats up, the CNS is disturbed, and paralysis of the respiratory centre is possible. Attention: heat stroke is not sunstroke; in the latter body temperature does not rise significantly.

t: Examination of the corpse: internal changes
n: In examination of the corpse, the internal changes in death from heat stroke and sunstroke are similar and non-specific. In the brain and meninges marked congestion, oedema and small perivascular haemorrhages are found. In the internal organs too there is congestion and small subserous haemorrhages. In the heart chambers and large vessels the blood is thick. Mucus collects in the airways, and the lungs take on a brownish hue because of the thick blood.

t: Rigor mortis, lividity and diagnostic difficulty
n: In death from heat stroke and sunstroke, rigor mortis develops quickly and is strong. Cadaveric lividity, however, appears late and is scanty. Remember: rigor strong, lividity scanty. The victims have no specific clinical signs, and doctors pay insufficient attention to the history, that is the circumstances of the case. For this reason, other clinical diagnoses are sometimes wrongly made.

t: Case analysis 1: death in hot conditions
n: The first case analysis. Situation: a worker who had been doing heavy work in a hot workshop, in clothing that does not pass air, stout or elderly, suddenly loses consciousness. Provoking factors: high temperature and humidity, absence of wind, heavy physical work, cardiovascular disease, obesity and old age. On the corpse, congestion of the brain and meninges, small perivascular haemorrhages, thick blood, rigor mortis rapid and strong, and lividity late and scanty. Question: are these signs characteristic of heat stroke or sunstroke? Answer: the morphological changes are similar, and there are no specific features.

t: Thermal burn: causes and features
n: A thermal burn arises when the temperature in and beneath the skin exceeds 45–50 °C. The nature of the burn depends on the type of source acting, its temperature, the duration of action and the injured area. This means that with the same exposure the result may differ. For example, with the same exposure the burn is deeper on areas with thin skin.

t: First- and second-degree burns
n: We consider first- and second-degree burns. In the second degree, blister fluid later becomes cloudy and thickens through coagulation of protein. On a corpse, the first degree sometimes appears as a yellowish, dry, slightly raised area. Attention: in a second-degree burn blister on a corpse, no blood emerges when the base is cut. This sign is important, because it is taken into account in assessing the burn.

t: Third- and fourth-degree burns
n: Now the third and fourth degrees. In degree III-A, necrosis is only in the superficial layer of the epidermis and dermis; the appearance is scab, granulation, then scar. In degree III-B, the epidermis and dermis undergo complete necrosis, and the surface is covered with a yellow or brownish scab; a scar remains. In degree IV, together with the skin, muscle, ligament and bone also undergo necrosis. Remember: degree IV forms only with the action of flame.

t: Superficial and deep burns; mixed degrees
n: Burns are divided into superficial and deep. Degrees I and II are superficial, and degrees III and IV are deep burns. In most victims, different degrees are found together in one injury: for example I–II, II–III or III–IV. A burn of degree I, II and III arises from all sources of high temperature, whereas degree IV forms only from the action of flame. Attention: do not confuse the superficial, that is I–II, and deep, that is III–IV, groups; link degree IV only with flame.

t: Quick question: degrees of burn
n: Quick questions on degrees of burn. First question: on the skin there is redness, slight swelling and pain, passing without trace in 3–4 days. Which degree is this? Second question: blisters with clear serous fluid, healing without a scar in 10–20 days. Which degree is this? Third question: hair and clothing are damaged, and there are traces of soot in the wound. Is the source flame or hot liquid? Fourth question: necrosis of muscle and bone was found. Which degree is this, and from which source may it be? Try to find the answers yourselves on the basis of the previous slides.

t: Determining the source of high temperature
n: From the features of a thermal burn, the source of high temperature can be determined. Hot liquid leaves a superficial burn in the form of run-off streaks, and hair and clothing are not damaged. Liquid, seeping under clothing and footwear, can scald covered areas too. Flame forms deep tongue-shaped wounds, hair and clothing are damaged, and traces of soot are found in the wound. A heated object, however, leaves a deep burn limited in surface, like a brand, its shape corresponding to the contact surface.

t: Simpson: scald and its signs
n: Signs of a scald. On immersion in boiling liquid a "liquid level" line forms, with splashing punctate foci, and with pouring run-off streaks in the direction of gravity. The streaks run under gravity, so they show the position of the victim at the time the liquid ran. Clothing holds liquid on the skin: the skin under wet clothing is severely damaged. In children, in an accidental, that is spill, scald, the border and depth are uneven. In forced immersion, however, a symmetrical "glove and stocking" shape and skin folds are preserved, and the depth is uniform.

t: Position of the victim and burn of the airways
n: The direction of the injury indicates the position of the victim. In a hot-liquid burn, the streaks are directed toward the low-lying parts of the body. In a flame burn, however, "tongues of flame" are directed toward the upper parts of the body. These wounds help to assess the position of the victim at the time of the incident. Burn of the airways is an injury characteristic only of the action of steam and hot gases. Deep burns often suppurate and heal very slowly; they leave a coarse scar that limits joint movement and may lead to disfigurement.

t: Simpson: burn severity and temperature limits
n: The severity of a burn depends on temperature and time. Complete necrosis of the epidermis occurs at 44 °C in 6 hours, at 60 °C in 5 seconds, and at 70 °C in less than 1 second. Injury by dry heat is called a burn, and by moist heat, that is hot water and steam, a scald. In the traditional classification, 1st degree is erythema and blister, 2nd degree the full thickness of the epidermis, 3rd degree down to the subcutaneous tissues, sometimes charring. The area of the burn, by the rule of nines and by Lund–Browder, may be more important than depth; risk factors: area, age and airway injury.

t: Burn area: the rule of nines
n: The area of a burn is estimated approximately by the "rule of nines"; this rule was proposed by A. Wallace in 1951. According to the table, the head and neck, arm, thigh, shin and heel are each 9%, the anterior surface of the trunk 18%, the posterior surface 18%, and the perineum 1%. The palm rule: the surface of one palm makes up approximately 1% of the total body surface. In forensic medical assessment, besides the degree of burn, the area occupied by the injury is also important.

t: The palm rule and writing the diagnosis as a fraction
n: The surface of the palm makes up approximately 1% of the total body surface; this is called the "palm rule". Special tables also exist for determining the area of a burn more precisely. In the diagnosis the burn is written as a fraction: in the numerator the area of the burn, in the denominator the degrees of burn. Attention: the numerator is not the denominator; do not confuse them. Example: 10 % / II or 30% (10%) / II–III. In brackets the area of the deeper burn is indicated.

t: Criteria of a life-threatening burn
n: If burn disease develops, even a burn of smaller area poses a threat to life. A burn of the airways, proceeding with oedema and narrowing of the glottis, is life-threatening. Criteria of a life-threatening burn: degree III–IV occupies more than 10 % of the body surface, degree III more than 15 %, and degree II more than 20 %. Attention: the deeper the burn, the smaller the threshold of area recognised as dangerous.

t: Burn disease
n: About burn disease. If a first-degree burn occupies more than 50% of the body surface, or second- to fourth-degree burns more than 10–15%, and death does not occur at once, changes arise in the internal organs. The severity of the disease depends on the depth and area of the burn and other factors. In its course there are four periods: shock, toxaemia, septicotoxaemia and convalescence. In young children the disease develops even with a small area and depth of burn and runs a more severe course than in adults. Concomitant diseases, especially in the elderly, lead to a more severe course of the disease.

t: The four periods of burn disease
n: Burn disease consists of four periods. The disease develops with an area of burn of degree I of more than 50%, of degrees II–IV of more than 10–15%, and if death is not rapid. The first period is burn shock: usually up to 1 day, sometimes 2–3 days, with a risk of death. Toxaemia lasts 1–2 weeks, with intoxication from protein breakdown. Septicotoxaemia lasts from 2–3 weeks to several months: suppuration, pneumonia, sepsis. In convalescence the wounds heal and function is restored. If in the shock period burn of the airways or carbon monoxide is added, the probability of death rises 2-fold or more. Attention: toxaemia is not septicotoxaemia.

t: Case analysis 2: scald by boiling water and flame burn
n: The second case analysis. Situation A: superficial burn in the form of run-off streaks, hair and clothing not damaged, the streaks directed to the lower parts of the body. Situation B: deep burn in tongue-like form, hair and clothing damaged, traces of soot in the wounds, "tongues of flame" pointing upward. Question: which situation is hot liquid and which the action of flame? What does the direction of the injury say about the position of the victim? Attention: if boiling water seeps in, areas covered by clothing or footwear may also be burned.

t: Vitality of the action of flame: the problem
n: Now the problem of the vitality of the action of flame. Victims in a fire more often die of carbon monoxide poisoning, and the corpse is afterwards charred by the action of flame. Therefore, in a corpse with traces of high temperature, it is necessary to determine whether the flame acted during life or after death. The decisive evidence: external injuries and microscopic examination of the skin, soft tissues and internal organs. Criteria: soot in the airways, carboxyhaemoglobin in the blood, and the "crow's feet" sign on the eyelids.

t: Signs of vitality: soot and carboxyhaemoglobin
n: The first of the signs of vitality is soot. If there is soot in the airways, oesophagus and stomach, the flame acted during life. Soot may also be found in the frontal and sphenoid sinuses, in leukocytes, and in the Kupffer cells of the liver. The second is carboxyhaemoglobin: after death it does not exceed 20%, and the blood may be in superficial vessels. With vital action, however, it may be up to 60%, and the blood is in the heart and deep vessels.

t: Taking samples and the "crow's feet" sign
n: The procedure for taking samples is important. To determine the vital action of flame, blood is taken from the heart chambers and deep vessels; in a superficial vessel carboxyhaemoglobin may be present even after death. To determine carboxymyoglobin, a sample from deeply lying muscles is taken to the laboratory. With vital action of flame the eyeballs are usually not damaged. In the upper part of the eyelid fold there is a burn and soot, but not at the base of the fold. When the eyelid skin is spread out, damaged and undamaged areas alternate. This is called the "crow's feet" sign.

t: Other signs: epidural haematoma and blisters
n: Other signs: epidural haematoma and blisters. An epidural haematoma formed from trauma is spindle-shaped and attached to the dura. A haematoma formed after death from flame, however, is crescent-shaped and not attached to the dura. There is also a difference in burn blisters: in vital burn blisters there is twice as much protein as in those formed after death.

t: Quick question: signs of vitality
n: Quick questions on signs of vitality. First question: if soot is found in the airways, oesophagus and stomach, when did the flame act? Answer: during life. Attention: carboxyhaemoglobin is also found after death, but does not exceed 20%; with vital action up to 60%. A traumatic epidural haematoma is spindle-shaped and attached to the dura; a post-mortem flame haematoma is crescent-shaped and not attached. In corpses after a fire, microscopic examination of the skin, soft tissues and internal organs is necessary.

t: The boxer posture and charring of the corpse
n: Under the action of flame, moisture evaporates in the corpse, proteins coagulate, and muscles become dense and shorten. As a result the limbs flex, and this is called the "boxer posture". The body may char completely. The skin becomes dense; if the effect is uneven, cracks and splits form in the skin. The chain is as follows: flame acts, moisture evaporates and protein coagulation occurs, muscles shorten, the boxer posture appears.

t: Simpson: the fire corpse, mechanisms of death and artefacts
n: Aims of examination of a fire corpse: identification of the person, establishing whether alive in the fire, the reason why he could not escape, and the cause and manner of death. Soot below the glottis and thermal injury of the airways indicate vitality. Carboxyhaemoglobin above 50 % is good evidence, while a low value does not exclude vitality. Most fire victims die not from burning but from inhalation of smoke, CO and hot gases. Artefacts include the boxer posture, splitting of burnt skin, heat fractures and epidural haemorrhage; the absence of signs of vitality distinguishes them from trauma.

t: Time of burning of the corpse and examination of the ash
n: The time of burning of a corpse depends on age: the corpse of an infant burns considerably faster than that of an adult. The time to turn to ash is 2–3 hours for an infant corpse and about 20 hours for an adult corpse. Crematorium conditions differ from the ordinary action of flame: with natural gas the time for an adult corpse is less than 1 hour, that is considerably shorter. To resolve questions of species, sex, age and others from the ash, forensic medical examination is carried out.

t: Case analysis 3: a corpse found after a fire
n: The third case analysis. Situation: after a fire a charred corpse was found, the limbs flexed, that is the "boxer posture". Question: did the flame act during life? The boxer posture is formed by densification and shortening of the muscles, that is moisture evaporates and protein coagulates. If there is soot in the airways, oesophagus and stomach, the flame acted during life. Carboxyhaemoglobin after death does not exceed 20%, during life up to 60%. Attention: if the epidural haematoma is spindle-shaped and attached to the dura, it is trauma; if crescent-shaped and not attached, post-mortem action of flame.

t: Stages of examination: examination of a fire corpse
n: The sequence of examination of a fire corpse is as follows. First, on external examination, soot is sought and the eyelids are checked for the "crow's feet" sign. Then blood is taken from the heart chambers and deep vessels. A muscle sample is taken from a deep layer; this is needed for carboxymyoglobin. Microscopic examination of the skin, soft tissues and internal organs, that is histology, is necessary. At the end a conclusion is drawn: whether the flame acted during life or after death.

t: Conclusion and key points
n: We summarise. In heat stroke, much heat is produced and little is given off. In sunstroke, body temperature does not rise significantly. The changes in the corpse are similar and non-specific. A burn has four degrees: I–III from all sources, IV only from flame. The area is assessed by the "rule of nines" and the palm rule, that is about 1%. Burn disease consists of four periods: burn shock, toxaemia, septicotoxaemia and convalescence. Signs of vitality: soot in the airways, carboxyhaemoglobin in the blood, carboxymyoglobin in muscle and "crow's feet" on the eyelids.
